lead: Software write blocking on Linux means telling the kernel to treat an evidence drive as read-only before anything can write to it. The Linux Write Blocker project adds a kernel patch and helper scripts for this, and the standard blockdev command and read-only mount options cover simpler cases.
use_when: You work on Linux and need to read an evidence drive without changing it, and a software method fits your lab policy.
You want to learn how write blocking works inside the Linux kernel.
You need to mount a file system from evidence for a quick look, with the lowest chance of writes.

features.title: Kernel patch
items: Changes the block layer so that write and discard requests to a device marked read-only are stopped
Works for requests from any kernel driver, without changing each storage driver
Does not need loop devices, which cannot easily stand in for devices that file systems use directly

features.title: Helper scripts
items: 01wrtblk_all marks all block devices except loop devices as read-only
wrtblk marks a named device and its parent as read-only, and wrtblk-disable sets them back to read-write
wrtblk-ioerr marks a device and its children as read-only, for faulty drives

features.title: udev rule
items: 01-forensic-readonly.rules marks new block devices read-only when they appear
It uses wrtblk, and wrtblk-ioerr for faulty drives
The paths in it are fixed, so review and adjust them before use

features.title: Standard Linux methods
items: blockdev --setro marks a device read-only, and blockdev --getro shows 1 for read-only
mount -o ro mounts a file system read-only
ro,noload stops ext3 and ext4 from replaying the journal at mount

requirements: A Linux computer and root rights. To use the project's patch you must apply it to a kernel source and compile your own kernel. The project says it was written for Linux 3.15.1 and works on some newer versions, and a version for Linux 4.10 exists. The blockdev command and mount options need no patch and are part of standard Linux.

steps.title: Read the project warnings
steps.text: Read the project's README before you start. It lists races, live system issues and bypass risks. Plan your method on paper and check your lab policy on software blockers.

steps.title: Stop automatic mounting
steps.text: Turn off automatic mounting and the automatic start of RAID, fake RAID and LVM volumes before you connect evidence. The project warns that the system may write to a drive before you mark it read-only. On live systems, protect all devices early in the boot.

steps.title: Set up the udev rule (optional)
steps.text: Local udev rules go in /etc/udev/rules.d and files must end in .rules. They are read in name order, so a name starting with 01 runs early. The project's 01-forensic-readonly.rules uses its helper scripts. Check the paths in it first.

steps.title: Mark the whole drive read-only
steps.text: Connect the drive, find its device name, and set the parent device read-only. Marking only a partition is not enough, says the project. The device name below is only an example.

steps.title: Check the flag
steps.text: Ask the system for the read-only status of the device. It prints 1 when the device is read-only. The manual notes that a file system that is already mounted read-write is not affected until it is remounted.

steps.title: Test with a known drive
steps.text: Before real evidence, test your setup with a spare drive. Hash it, try to write to it as a test, and hash it again. The hash must not change. Record the test in your lab notes and repeat it when the system or kernel changes.

steps.title: Image or mount read-only
steps.text: Make the image from the whole device with an imaging tool. If you must mount, add the read-only options. For ext3 and ext4 add noload, so the journal is not replayed. For ntfs-3g the project gives the ro option.

options.what: Marks a device read-only. Use the parent device, not only a partition.
Prints 1 if the device is read-only, 0 if not.
Mounts read-only and, for ext3 and ext4, skips the journal replay that would write to the device.
Project helper that marks a device and its child devices read-only, for faulty drives.

cases.title: Labs without a hardware blocker
cases.why: Where policy allows it, a tested software method lets you read a drive on a Linux computer.

cases.title: Forensic live systems
cases.why: Setting every device read-only early in the boot lowers the risk that the live system writes to evidence.

cases.title: Mounting a file system for a quick look
cases.why: Read-only mount options with the device flag reduce the chance of writes such as journal replay.

cases.title: Research and teaching
cases.why: The project includes discussion and validation work in its research and validation folders, so students can see how a blocker is tested.

strengths: Free and open source, with code you can read.
Blocks at the block layer, so it does not rely on each file system driver to respect read-only.
The project reports no loss of speed after applying the patch.
The same ideas work in many Linux forensic tools and live systems.
limits: Software blocking must be tested on your own system before you trust it. A passing test on one computer or kernel does not prove another one is safe.
It is not a substitute for a hardware write blocker where your policy, standards or court practice require one.

The project warns that any software blocker can be bypassed by another program. The patch does not cover SCSI commands sent through the SG_IO interface, which includes some hdparm and sg3_utils commands.
A race is possible: the system may write to a drive before you mark it read-only. Disable automatic mounting first.
A read-only mount is not enough on its own. For example, ext3 and ext4 still replay the journal unless you add noload.
The kernel patch needs a custom kernel build. The project's udev rule and scripts have fixed paths you must check.
Creating a partition can re-trigger the udev rule and mark the disk read-only again, which can disturb partitioning work.

works_with.note: A live system that includes write blocking

sources_note: Written in our own words from the Linux Write Blocker project's README and the Linux manual pages.
